newsitem.title: MEXICO: Electoral supervisor sees clean Mexican elections.
newsitem.headline: Electoral supervisor sees clean Mexican elections.

text.p: The man running Mexico's key midterm elections promised on Tuesday a clean, honest vote with none of the shenanigans that have plagued previous polls.
In an interview with Reuters, Jose Woldenberg, the president of Mexico's newly independent Federal Electoral Institute (IFE) outlined painstaking efforts to ensure clean elections next Sunday.

Mexicans will choose new federal deputies, a quarter of the Senate, six state governors and, for the first time in decades, the Mexico City mayor. The post was previously filled by a presidential nominee.
"We've done our part to guarantee the vote will be secret and secure," Woldenberg said. "For the first time we will have elections with no government participation."

The 52.2 million registered voters must show a one-time use photo credential, appear on a computerized list at their regional voting site and have their right thumb stamped with indelible ink to prevent duplicate voting.
Election observers will be on duty at each polling booth to watch over the proceedings.
Apart from these efforts, the IFE has launched a national campaign with billboards and television advertisements to persuade voters that their vote will be "free and secret."
Many Mexicans still remember highly controversial votes such as the 1988 presidential election, when the computer collecting the results halted when the opposition was ahead.
It then came back up hours later, showing the ruling party candidate winning. The government denied any wrongdoing but ordered the ballot papers burned to prevent a recount.
Common suspicion of electoral results is reflected in the refrain: "The opposition candidate party may win the elections, but the ruling party will continue to govern."
The Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) has governed Mexico for 68 unbroken years.
Until last November, the IFE was led by the Interior Minister but it is now run by nine independent citizen "councillors" picked by consensus among the main parties.
Woldenberg said he estimated an election turnout similar to the average of about 78 percent in recent years.
"These elections come at a moment of political transition for Mexico, changing from a system of almost one-party rule to an authentic party system," he said.
He said the IFE has clashed with the different parties, including the PRI, since becoming independent but has not had "systematic confrontations."

Nonetheless, the parties have registered about 110 complaints with the IFE, accusing rivals of tearing down campaign signs and other minor violations. The IFE studies the cases and decides sanctions, Woldenberg said.
